rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah’s message serves the addressees rather than his own financial interest; he is self-sufficient in their matter, and listening benefits them by protecting them from God’s wrath, while God will reward him either way.
rows.anchor: His recompense rests with God Who will not deprive him from it whether they listen to him or not.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The arrogant opponents object to sharing company with humble believers and implicitly demand that Noah expel them; lacking an argument against his message, they use this as a face-saving excuse.
rows.anchor: these arrogant people had nothing to say to deny Noah’s (sws) message and call.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah says rank depends on character, not family or lineage; he does not know the believers’ past deeds, which God will judge, while their present profession of faith and fear is evident.
rows.anchor: whether a person is of high status or low depends on his character and not on his family and lineage

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means that if the opponents understood status to rest on conduct rather than wealth or social rank, they would have made Noah’s argument; their arrogance blocks acceptance of truth.
rows.anchor: This arrogant notion has become a hindrance for them to accept the truth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah will not abandon the believers to gain acceptance; as an open warner he has discharged his duty, and whoever rejects faith alone bears responsibility for that failure.
rows.anchor: As an open warner, he has discharged his responsibility. He who does not accept faith will alone be responsible for this lapse.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording indicates that Noah had already been threatened with stoning and ignored it; now the nation declares emphatically that the threat will be carried out.
rows.anchor: earlier on too they had threatened to stone Noah (sws) to death but he ignored them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the nation’s final declaration and losing hope that they would believe, Noah supplicates to God, following the well-known practice of messengers.
rows.anchor: he supplicated to God in these words

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic word fatḥan signals that Noah asks for decisive help and victory, which entails destroying the nation that denied its messenger and saving his companions.
rows.anchor: shows that Noah (sws) supplicated for the victory and help that necessarily culminates in the destruction of a nation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Noah prayed at the right time, God immediately accepted his supplication: a storm drowned the nation while Noah and his followers were saved.
rows.anchor: Since Noah’s (sws) supplication was uttered at the right time, it was immediately accepted.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shahn means filling; here it describes the ship and the things Noah was instructed to load. God had the vessel built with what its passengers needed to survive the storm.
rows.anchor: means “to fill something.” Here it qualifies the ship and refers to things

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated closing verses return to the demand for a sign: Noah’s historical account itself is a great sign for those who seek one.
rows.anchor: The implication is that if these people want a sign

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most remain stubborn and evade faith with excuses, so even the greatest sign will not make them believe.
rows.anchor: Their majority will not accept faith even after observing the greatest of signs.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God can seize Prophet Muhammad’s rejecters at any time because He is dominant, yet gives them respite through His mercy.
rows.anchor: Prophet Muḥammad’s Lord can seize his rejecters anytime because He is dominant. However, He is giving them respite since He is also merciful.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Where the previous sūrah detailed Moses and Noah but briefly mentioned intervening nations, this sūrah details those nations’ dealings with their messengers and their fates in historical order, ending each account with a refrain.
rows.anchor: The sequence adopted is historical and at the end of every anecdote the repetitive verses occur.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As in 26:105, denying one messenger means denying all, since they bring the same message; the Qur’an therefore rejects claims of faith that discriminate among God’s messengers, including those of the People of the Book.
rows.anchor: The word “messengers” occurs in the plural for the reason stated in verse 105.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hud was their own brother, not a stranger; they knew his impeccable life, so treating him as a liar or fabricator reflects their utter misfortune.
rows.anchor: The verse says that Hūd (sws) was their brother and not a stranger to them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hud’s repeated exhortation to fear God and obey him also rebukes people who evade his call and will not even listen.
rows.anchor: Moreover, it also carries rebuke for those

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hud tells them that his message costs them nothing and is free of charge.
rows.anchor: what he is presenting to them is not going to cost them anything. It is free of charge.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rīʿ means a high ground visible from afar.
rows.anchor: means a high ground that can be spotted from afar.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Āyah here means a sign or monument.
rows.anchor: here refers to a sign or a monument.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maṣāniʿ refers to palaces, castles, and large structures.
rows.anchor: is used for palaces, castles and large structures.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In eloquent Arabic, laʿalla can mean as if.
rows.anchor: In eloquent Arabic, the word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hud condemns building monuments and palaces for display or entertainment instead of need: the wealthy build as though life were endless, treating this world as their destination and neglecting preparation for the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: should be constructed to fulfil needs and not to show off and boast about.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hud addresses his nation’s leaders: neglect of the Hereafter yields distorted social priorities, with the wealthy competing in luxury while thousands of poor people lack shelter and suffer from cold or heat.
rows.anchor: When the Hereafter is disregarded and all attention is focused on this world, society and civilization exhibit wrong priorities.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hud identifies two causes of this disorder: building useless landmarks for pomp and seeking to live forever.
rows.anchor: Hūd (sws) has pointed out two causes of this disorder

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says these causes apply equally to his own nation and promises further discussion of useful and useless construction in his exegesis of Sūrah al-Naml.
rows.anchor: These causes are equally applicable to our own nation as well.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hud calls wars of domination and subjugation disorder; war is permissible only to curb evil, and righteous jihād is defensive or roots out persecution, thus supporting truth and God’s word.
rows.anchor: This is only allowed when the purpose is to check and curb evil.
